prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Beginning, The, And

outputs.L1:
Beginning to dangle beneath the wind that blows from the undermined wood, I feel the great pulley grind, the thread I cling to lengthen, and let me soar and spin down into marble—hooked and weightlessly happy—where the squared sun shines back equally from all four sides, out of stone and years of dazzling labor.

At last, I land among men who cut, with power saws, a Parian whiteness and, chewing slow tobacco, their eyebrows like frost, shunt house-sized blocks, lash them to cables, and send them heavenward into small-town banks, into the columns and statues of government buildings, but mostly into graves.

I mount my monument and rise, slowly and spinningly, from the white-gloved men toward the hewn sky, out of the basement of light—sadly lifted through time’s blinding layers, perhaps upon my tombstone, in which the original shape Michelangelo believed was in every rock upon earth is heavily stirring, surprised to be an angel, to be awakened in North Georgia by the ponderous play of men with ten-ton blocks.

Yet it is no more surprised than I am to feel sadness fall away, as though I myself were rising from stone, held by a thread in midair: badly cut, local-looking, and wholly uninspired—not a masterwork, nor even worth seeing at all, but the spirit of this place just the same, felt here as joy.
outputs.L2:
As I start to hang below the gusts coming out of the weakened forest, I sense the huge hoist straining. The line holding me pays out, lowering me in a wheeling, floating descent toward the marble. I am caught there, light as air and strangely delighted, in a place where the square blaze of the sun reflects evenly from every side—off the stone and off the long years of brilliant work.

At last I come down among workers who use power saws to carve Parian-white stone. They chew tobacco slowly, their brows pale as frost, shifting blocks as large as houses, fastening them to cables, and lifting them upward. Those blocks will become small-town bank fronts, the pillars and figures of public buildings, and, more than anything else, grave markers.

I climb onto my own memorial and begin to ascend, turning slowly away from the men in white gloves, up toward the cut-out sky, out of that cellar of brightness. I am carried sorrowfully through the dazzling strata of time, perhaps on my own headstone. Inside it, the first form that Michelangelo thought existed within every stone on earth is moving heavily, astonished to find itself becoming an angel—awakened in North Georgia by the massive handling of ten-ton blocks.

Yet it is no more astonished than I am to feel grief drop away, as if I too were being lifted from rock, suspended in the air by a single thread: crudely carved, plainly local, entirely lacking inspiration, not a masterpiece, not even something worth stopping to look at—and still, all the same, the true spirit of this place, experienced here as joy.
outputs.L3:
The poem presents the speaker’s imagined descent into a marble quarry, a vast and dazzling world of white stone. Suspended as if by a thread, the speaker moves downward into a space that feels both dangerous and strangely beautiful. The whiteness of the marble surrounds everything, creating an almost otherworldly atmosphere in which the quarry becomes more than a workplace; it becomes a place of vision and transformation.

Within this setting, workers are shown cutting, moving, and hoisting enormous blocks of marble. Their labor connects the raw material of the earth to the structures and objects that will later shape public and private life. These blocks may become banks, government buildings, statues, or graves. In this way, the poem links the quarry to both power and memory: marble is used to create monuments of wealth and authority, but also tombstones that mark death and preserve remembrance.

The poem also reflects on the artistic and symbolic possibilities hidden inside the stone. It recalls the idea associated with Michelangelo that figures already exist within blocks of marble, waiting to be released by the sculptor. This gives the quarried stone a sense of mystery and potential. The marble is not merely material to be extracted and used; it seems to contain forms, histories, and meanings that are waiting to emerge.

As the speaker experiences this descent, there is a powerful emotional shift. Sadness falls away, and the encounter with the quarry becomes unexpectedly joyful. What might have seemed cold, heavy, or oppressive is instead transformed into something uplifting. The speaker feels changed by the brightness, the scale, and the strange beauty of the place.

Ultimately, the poem suggests that beauty and meaning do not belong only to perfect or classical forms. Even imperfect, ordinary, or local shapes can express the spirit of a place. The quarry, with its labor, rough stone, and unfinished blocks, becomes a source of artistic and emotional insight. Through this vision, the poem celebrates the ability of material things—even those still in their raw state—to hold memory, identity, and joy.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores transcendence, labor, and mortality through a speaker’s imagined movement into and out of a North Georgia marble quarry. At first, the quarry appears as a place of depth, pressure, and darkness: a wound in the earth where human beings descend to cut and raise stone. This descent suggests more than a physical journey. It becomes a meditation on the hidden sources of beauty and permanence, on the hard work required to bring buried material into the world, and on the nearness of death that accompanies any encounter with stone, graves, and the earth itself.

The quarry workers occupy a central role in this vision. Their labor transforms raw marble into the structures of public and private life: banks, government buildings, monuments, and tombs. In their hands, the stone moves from nature into culture, from the mountain into the city, from the depths of the earth into the visible forms by which communities define power, memory, and value. The marble becomes part of institutions meant to endure, but it also becomes part of burial and mourning. Thus the same material that supports civic authority and economic life also marks human mortality.

Yet the poem does not treat this transformation as merely practical or industrial. The speaker sees in the workers’ activity a kind of spiritual passage. The stone rises from the quarry and takes on forms that are not perfect, heavenly, or abstract, but earthly and ordinary. Banks and government buildings may be flawed human creations; graves may remind us of loss rather than triumph. Still, these forms carry something of the place from which they came. They preserve the quarry’s presence, its whiteness, weight, and silence, even after the marble has been cut, polished, and relocated.

By imagining both descent and ascent, the poem suggests that transcendence is not an escape from the material world but a deeper recognition of it. Spirit is not found apart from labor, stone, death, or local geography. Instead, it emerges through them. The North Georgia marble, shaped by workers and placed within human institutions and burial grounds, becomes a vessel for the spirit of the region. In the end, the poem discovers joy not in perfection, but in the imperfect forms of ordinary life—forms that nevertheless bear the marks of human effort, earthly beauty, and communal memory.
outputs.L5:
**The Beginning and the Journey**

The beginning is often the most important part of any journey. It is the moment when an idea first appears, when a decision is made, and when the first step is taken. Every story, dream, and achievement starts with a beginning.

The beginning may feel exciting, but it can also feel uncertain. People often wonder if they are ready, if they have enough knowledge, or if they will succeed. And yet, without beginning, nothing can grow or change. The first step may be small, but it creates movement.

The beginning teaches courage. And with courage comes progress. Even when the path is difficult, each step forward brings experience and understanding. The journey may not always be perfect, but it becomes meaningful because someone was brave enough to start.

In the end, the beginning is more than just a starting point. It is the foundation of everything that follows. And every great success begins with one simple step.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem in the style of James Dickey about visiting a marble quarry in North Georgia, with imagery of cranes, cables, tombstones, government buildings, Michelangelo, and a feeling of unexpected joy.
counterfactuals.output:
At Tate, in the white wound of the mountain,  
I stood where the earth had been opened  
not like a grave  
but like a morning.

All around me the cranes leaned out  
over the quarry’s terrible brightness,  
their long necks black against the sky,  
their cables humming  
with the weight of something older than names.  
Blocks of marble rose slowly from the pit,  
dripping light,  
as if the whole hill had decided  
to give up its bones.

There was dust on my shoes,  
white as flour,  
white as ash,  
white as the faces of tombstones  
waiting in rows somewhere beyond the cutting shed—  
beloved mother,  
infant son,  
veteran of a war no one living can remember—  
all of them already sleeping  
inside this hard, cold radiance.

And yet I was glad.

I do not know why joy came to me there,  
among the saws, the derricks, the warning bells,  
the men in hard hats shouting upward  
to the operator hidden in glass,  
while the cable tightened  
and the great stone shuddered loose  
from its bed.

Maybe it was the way the marble held the sun  
without burning.  
Maybe it was knowing that courthouses, capitols,  
post offices with their stern steps and columns,  
the solemn houses of government  
where men argue the shape of justice,  
had begun like this—  
as silence under a Georgia hill.

Maybe it was Michelangelo,  
far off in time,  
standing before such whiteness  
and seeing not rock  
but a shoulder, a throat,  
the fierce bent head of David  
still trapped and waiting,  
the angel not yet delivered  
from the block.

Down in the quarry water gathered  
green and deep,  
a secret lake at the bottom of labor.  
The cables sang again.  
The cranes dipped and lifted.  
A slab swung slowly through the air,  
huge, helpless, shining,  
and every man near it stepped back  
with the reverence of the living  
before what may outlast them.

I thought of my own name  
one day cut into stone,  
my dates bitten cleanly beneath it,  
and still the happiness rose in me—  
unasked, unreasonable,  
like a spring breaking through limestone.

For there, where the mountain was being taken apart  
piece by piece,  
nothing seemed destroyed.  
Everything seemed released:  
buildings, angels, monuments, thresholds,  
the cool forehead of a statue,  
the last white pillow of the dead.

And above the quarry  
the North Georgia sky opened wide,  
blue and ordinary,  
while the cranes kept lifting  
the buried brightness of the world  
into the astonished air.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a long, single-stanza lyric poem narrated by someone dangling above a marble quarry, watching workers cut and hoist huge white stone blocks, ending with the speaker feeling like the rough local spirit of the place.
counterfactuals.output:
I hang in the wind above the marble quarry,  
a fly caught in the blue web of noon,  
my boots tasting nothing, my hands gone tight  
on the cable that creaks like an old throat,  
and below me the mountain lies opened  
as if some god had laid a white animal down  
and peeled back its hide to show the luminous bone.  
Men move there, small as quarry ants,  
their shirts darkened by sweat, their caps pale with dust,  
their voices rising in brief sparks  
and vanishing under the scream of the saws.  
The wire bites through the cliff with a song  
too thin for grief, too steady for anger,  
and the whole cut face trembles  
as if remembering a winter buried in it,  
as if the stone were full of sleeping weather  
that did not want to be woken.  
Water runs silver along the grooves,  
slurry gathers in milky pools,  
and the sun strikes every wet surface  
until the pit is a basin of broken moons.  
I watch the wedges driven in,  
iron tongues persuading the mountain,  
I watch the block loosen with a sigh  
too deep to belong to men,  
a sigh from under the village, under the vineyards,  
under the graves where quarry dust settles  
on names already half-erased.  
Then the cranes begin their patient lifting,  
chains clattering like harness on giants,  
hooks swinging, men shouting, palms raised,  
and one enormous white block, squared and raw,  
leaves the bed it has kept for ages,  
rises slowly into air,  
dripping water, shedding grit,  
the wound beneath it bright and fresh.  
It floats there for a moment,  
not stone but a thought too heavy for the earth,  
a piece of cold daylight hauled from darkness,  
a future column, stair, saint, table, tomb,  
a face not yet carved looking everywhere at once.  
The workers guide it with ropes,  
lean back hard with their whole bodies,  
feet skidding in white mud,  
their muscles drawing black lines under the skin,  
and I, hanging higher than prayer,  
feel the swing of my own suspended weight,  
feel the mountain’s breath push through me,  
feel the dust enter my mouth  
and grind softly between my teeth.  
All around, the cliffs glare without mercy,  
terraces cut into the old slope  
like pages torn from a sacred book,  
and the valley below keeps its green silence,  
olive trees silvering in the heat,  
goats nosing the scrub,  
a road curling down toward roofs and bells,  
toward kitchens where bread is broken  
and no one speaks of how the mountain bleeds  
except as work, except as wages,  
except as the white powder on a father’s cuffs.  
I think of the dead embedded here,  
not bodies, but hours,  
the hammer-strokes of grandfathers,  
the coughs of boys who grew old in dust,  
the nicknames shouted across the pit,  
the cheap wine drunk in shade,  
the curses thrown at broken blades,  
the lullabies carried home on shoulders aching  
from a day spent cutting brightness out of stone.  
The cable sways; I sway with it.  
The sky is an emptied bowl above me,  
the quarry an altar below,  
and every block hauled up seems to pass through my ribs,  
leaving me more hollow, more white,  
more roughly quarried from myself.  
I no longer know whether I am watching  
or being watched by the cut mountain,  
whether the men below are freeing stone  
or teaching it the shape of their endurance.  
Their saws keep singing; their cranes keep bowing;  
the great blocks rise and turn in the light  
like mute, unbaptized gods.  
Dust climbs toward me in slow veils,  
settles on my hair, my lashes, my tongue,  
clothes me in the quarry’s own weather,  
and when the wind comes hard from the broken face  
I answer it without words,  
with a throat of gravel, with knuckles of lime,  
with the stubborn breath of ledge and thorn,  
until, dangling there above the men and the stone,  
I feel myself no longer a visitor, no longer a body afraid of falling,  
but the coarse tutelary thing of this place,  
the local daemon, hoarse and white with dust,  
rough as the mountain’s opened heart.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a Southern American free verse poem that transforms an industrial quarry scene—power saws, tobacco-chewing men, Parian whiteness, blocks sent to banks, columns, statues, and graves—into a meditation on death, art, and transcendence.
counterfactuals.output:
At sunup the quarry opens  
like a white wound in the hill,  
and the men come down into it  
with their lunch pails, their hard hats,  
their tobacco tucked in the jaw  
like a dark thought they will not spit out yet.

Power saws sing their iron hymns,  
shrill and steady,  
biting the morning into dust.  
All day the blades worry the ledge,  
and the ledge gives back  
its Parian whiteness—  
not snow, not bone,  
but something kin to both.

The men know stone  
the way a widow knows a room:  
by weight, by silence,  
by what is missing when a block is gone.  
They pry it loose,  
chain it, hoist it,  
send it groaning up toward daylight  
as if raising Lazarus  
piece by numbered piece.

From here it travels north and east,  
down rail lines, over brown rivers,  
into the clean hands of banks,  
where it stands polished and cool  
beneath brass lamps and whispered loans;  
into courthouses,  
where columns lift their pale throats  
and pretend justice has no dust on her shoes;  
into museums and mansions,  
where statues rise from the same old earth  
and learn to look away.

And some of it goes  
to the graveyards.

There, under cedar and rain,  
the stone takes on names,  
takes on dates,  
takes on lambs, angels, clasped hands,  
the chiseled promises  
of Resurrection and Beloved,  
of Mother, Father, Infant Son—  
words the dead cannot read  
but the living lean on  
like fence posts in a field gone under.

I have seen those slabs after stormlight,  
gleaming at dusk  
with a milk-white mercy,  
as if the hill itself  
had been cut open  
to make a door.

Maybe art is only this:  
the hard thing broken  
until it bears a human face.  
Maybe death is only this:  
the body quarried from its breath,  
loaded out in darkness,  
sent on ahead  
to some far building  
we have not yet imagined.

Still, the men work on.  
They spit brown into the dust.  
They wipe their necks with red rags.  
They laugh low,  
curse the heat,  
measure the seam,  
set the saw again.

Above them, buzzards circle  
in the blue cathedral of noon,  
black commas turning  
over the unfinished sentence  
of the world.

And below,  
where the blade enters  
and water runs white as baptism,  
the stone shines back—  
cold, patient,  
almost holy—  
waiting to be bank,  
pillar, angel,  
threshold,  
name,

waiting to be lifted  
from the broken hill  
and made into something  
that stands.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I need a poem imitating mid-20th-century American nature/industrial poetry: the speaker is suspended by a thread over a North Georgia marble quarry and imagines becoming an awkward angel or tombstone rising out of stone.
counterfactuals.output:
**Over a North Georgia Quarry**

Lower me, inch by inch,  
into the white noon of the pit,  
where the cranes stand still  
like long-legged birds  
that have forgotten water.

The cable hums above me—  
one black thread  
sewn through the blue shirt of heaven—  
and I hang from it,  
awkward, unfinished,  
a man not yet fallen  
and not yet saved.

Below, the marble opens  
its cold, enormous book.  
Every ledge is a page  
the mountain has been writing  
before there were hands  
to turn it into names.

Men move down there  
small as dark commas,  
drilling their thunder  
into the old white silence.  
Dust lifts from the cut stone  
like breath from a sleeping animal.

I think: if the thread broke,  
I would not fall as a man falls.  
I would enter the quarry  
slowly, strangely—  
arms spread wide  
in the foolish geometry of fear—  
and for one bright second  
be mistaken for an angel,

not a good one,  
not a burning one,  
but some heavy, work-worn spirit  
called up by dynamite  
from the ribs of Georgia.

Or else I would rise,  
already dead,  
out of the marble below—  
a blank tombstone  
pushing through its own grave,  
my face weathered smooth  
before it was carved,

my name still hidden  
deep in the white vein  
where the mountain keeps  
all our endings  
cool, hard, and shining.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an imagistic, meditative poem about marble being quarried and lifted by pulleys, connecting the stone to Michelangelo’s belief about hidden forms, monuments, graves, sadness falling away, and joy in a specific place.
counterfactuals.output:
In Carrara, the mountain opens  
its white throat to morning.

Iron teeth mark the seam.  
Dust lifts like breath  
from an old god’s sleep.

The marble waits—  
not mute, but inward,  
holding its brightness  
under centuries of stone.

Ropes tighten.  
Pulleys turn slowly  
against the blue,  
and a block rises  
from the wound of the hill,

heavy as a cathedral,  
pale as a bone  
washed clean by rain.

Michelangelo said  
the figure was already there—  
the hand, the face,  
the bent knee emerging  
when all that was not mercy  
fell away.

So the mountain gives up  
its hidden bodies:

saints for domes,  
angels for tombs,  
names cut deep  
above the quiet dead.

Even sorrow is carved  
by removal.

Chip by chip,  
the dark excess loosens;  
grief slides down  
in powder and fragments  
to the quarry floor.

And somewhere below,  
in the white streets of Carrara,  
a bell leans into noon.

The lifted stone  
swings briefly in the sun,  
and for one bright instant  
it is not monument,  
not grave,

but joy—  
uncovered, weightless,  
held in the open air.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
